title: Do You Really Swallow 8 Spiders a Year in Your Sleep?

segments.chapter: You swallow 8 spiders a year in your sleep

lines.say: Eight spiders a year. That's how many you supposedly swallow in your sleep.
Mouth open. Eight legs walking in. Nope.
I'm sleeping in a helmet tonight.
Spider experts say there's no solid evidence it happens.
And that eight a year number? Somebody made it up.
That's one of eight bug stories. The last one has no head.
Why no spiders? To them, you're a giant, snoring earthquake.
Your breathing sends out vibrations. To a spider, that's probably danger.
Could one wander in? Maybe. Pure random chance. Helmet off.

segments.chapter: Daddy longlegs have the deadliest venom on Earth

lines.say: Next, in your basement: the deadliest venom on Earth. Supposedly.
Problem one. Daddy longlegs is three different animals.
The harvestman? Not even a spider. Zero venom glands.
The crane fly? A giant mosquito look-alike. It doesn't bite.
The cellar spider is the real spider. With real venom.
It shakes another spider's web. Then eats the owner.
But its venom? Studies say it's pretty mild.
And nobody's ever shown it's deadly to people.
Busted. The scariest thing about it is the rumor.
My roommate vacuums them up anyway. Rude.
The next one's named after a body part. Yours.

segments.chapter: Earwigs crawl into your ears while you sleep

lines.say: Earwigs. They crawl into your ear while you sleep.
Then burrow into your brain. That's the old story.
My roommate sleeps with earplugs because of this bug.
So one bug scientist checked. Ten centuries of writing.
The result? One single report.
Busted. Your ears are very safe.
At night it's out eating aphids and other bugs.
And the mom guards her eggs. Then feeds her babies.
Trap one in your clothes, and it might pinch. That's it.
The next one's in your kitchen. They say nothing can kill it.

segments.chapter: Cockroaches would survive a nuclear bomb

lines.say: The cockroach. After a nuclear bomb, it's the last thing standing.
It is tough. Six to fifteen times more radiation than you.
But the fruit fly on your banana? Even tougher.
Remember that fly. It comes back.
Ants that dig deep nests would likely outlast it too.
Roaches in the rubble after the bomb? No documented evidence.
And once everything else is gone? No food. No roaches.
Busted. Tough, yes. Nuke-proof, no.
My roommate's doomsday plan was: be a cockroach. Awkward.
Four stories down. The next four sound fake, and they're real.
Starting with a spider that really did land in a girl's mouth.
Spiders can fly. No wings.
Real. It's called ballooning.
A baby spider climbs up high. Rear end to the sky.
Out come the silk threads. And the wind takes it.
Some ride the wind for miles.
Darwin watched them land on his ship. Sixty miles from shore.
In a lab, an electric field lifted them. No wind needed.
And that girl? Windy day. Grassy field. One blew right in.
Flying spiders. The helmet's back on.
The next one just landed on your sandwich. It's tasting it.

segments.chapter: A fly tastes your food with its feet

lines.say: A fly tastes your food with its feet.
Its feet can tell sugar water from plain water.
Feet touch something sweet, and out comes the mouth.
No chewing. It spits on solid food to turn it to soup.
It can even throw up on it, to speed things up.
Don't zap one near your food, either. The body can burst.
Real. Every landing is a taste test.
My roommate still ate the sandwich.
Its tiny cousin on your banana? It's been to space.

segments.chapter: Fruit flies went to space before any human

lines.say: Fruit flies went to space before any human. And came back.
Nineteen forty seven. A rocket launches from New Mexico.
It climbs more than sixty miles up.
The passengers? A bunch of fruit flies.
Before monkeys. Before dogs. Before us.
Scientists wanted to know what space radiation does to life.
The capsule parachuted back safely. No mutations found.
Told you that fly was tougher than a roach.
Real. Respect the fruit fly. Then toss the banana.
Last story. The one I promised. It has no head.

segments.chapter: A cockroach can live for weeks without its head

lines.say: A cockroach can live for weeks without its head.
Real. Here's how.
It doesn't breathe through its head.
It breathes through tiny holes along its body.
Its blood pressure is low. So the neck just clots shut.
No brain needed for the basics. It stands. It moves.
It can go weeks on its last meal.
And the head? It keeps waving its antennae. For hours.
So what finally gets it? No mouth. Thirst, or infection.
My roommate just left the room.
So. Eight spiders a year, in your sleep? Still zero.
Four stories busted. Four real. One helmet. Staying on.
Watch this next. Kill It or Keep It. Bugs you should never kill.

_engagement: 11/10 v4 (coordinator; research 72 + 73): NO quiz framing. Each story opens on the claim as a concrete statement with the animal on screen, gives the reveal early (story 1 by ~0:11), then the why. The MYTH/TRUE board stamp is the reveal. No 'Myth or true?', no spoken countdowns. Two pause-and-reveal beats only (a 1.3 s '?' ring, no numbers): spiders fly and the headless roach. Story 1 is <= 30 s. Count + order + open loop at ~0:16 ('eight bug stories; the last one has no head', kept on screen as a chip until it pays off). Order: 4 busted, a midpoint re-hook ('Four stories down. The next four sound fake, and they're real.'), then 4 real, ending on the headless roach. A second loop (the girl with a spider in her mouth) opens at the midpoint and pays off in story 5. Every item ends on the next item's stake. Character beats every 30-40 s: Meatball's helmet (on at 0:06, off at 0:28, back on when spiders fly, kept at the end) and five roommate lines. Ending: callback to the opening, recap board, then 'watch this next' naming Kill It or Keep It. Narration avoids the channel's banned words.
end_ask: 3 BUGS IN YOUR HOUSE YOU SHOULD NEVER KILL
